latest_rss.title: Low Trust Stymies Emergence of a ‘Chinese Palantir’
latest_rss.summary:
Executive Summary:




Data is central to the People’s Republic of China’s (PRC) economic, governance, and military ambitions, but its data ecosystem remains fragmented and institutionally underdeveloped.



The PRC’s efforts to address this challenge circle the need for a platform like Palantir that can integrate disparate datasets into more standardized and usable systems.



Chinese firms have developed products and services analogous to some of Palantir’s capabilities, including data-integration platforms, ontologies, knowledge graphs, and military AI tools. Yet a single national champion able to perform across sensitive government, military, and commercial systems has not emerged.



The primary obstacle facing a “Chinese Palantir” is the PRC’s low-trust environment. Cybersecurity risks, bureaucratic rivalries, and political sensitivity around data prevent any single company from being trusted with the cross-institutional access needed to rival Palantir’s expansive capabilities.

latest_rss.summary: China's Pinglu Canal officially opens to navigation on Wednesday, giving southwest China a shortcut to the coast and overseas markets. The 134.2-kilometer waterway connects the Xijiang River shipping network with the Beibu Gulf in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region.Designed for vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the canal marks the completion of a major river-to-sea transport project, bringing together navigation engineering, ecological protection and regional logistics.The canal was built at a cost of 72.7 billion yuan (about $10.75 billion).Engineering a route from river to seaThe canal connects the Xijiang River system with the Beibu Gulf through a network of waterways and ship locks.Three double-line ship locks at Madao, Qishi and Qingnian are key parts of the navigation system. latest_rss.title: Chinese scientists build world’s smallest CT scanner, weighing just 6kg
latest_rss.summary:
Chinese researchers have developed the world’s smallest CT scanner, a portable device designed to produce images of tiny fossils and archaeological relics.
Built by the Shandong province-based Rayim, the Xtomo-Cube is about the size of a desktop speaker and weighs just 6kg (13.2lbs).
